title: Double-entry bookkeeping
text: Double-entry bookkeeping records every movement of money twice: once as a debit to one account and once as a credit to another. Because the two sides must always be equal, the books carry a built-in error check. If the totals ever disagree, something was recorded incorrectly and an accountant knows to go looking for it.

title: Idempotency keys
text: An idempotency key is a unique token a client attaches to a request so the server can recognize retries. If a payment request times out and the client sends it again with the same key, the server returns the original result instead of charging the customer twice. Payment APIs rely on this because networks drop responses far more often than people expect.

title: Compound interest
text: Compound interest means earning interest on previously earned interest. A deposit growing at five percent per year does not simply add the same amount each year; the base keeps getting larger. Over long horizons this snowball effect dominates, which is why saving early matters more than saving large amounts later.

title: APR versus APY
text: The annual percentage rate states the yearly cost of borrowing without accounting for compounding. The annual percentage yield includes the effect of compounding, so it is always equal to or higher than the APR for the same loan or deposit. Lenders like to advertise the APR on loans, while banks prefer to quote the APY on savings accounts.

title: The order book
text: An order book is the list of every outstanding buy and sell order for a security, organized by price. Buy orders are called bids and sell orders are called asks. The highest bid and the lowest ask form the top of the book, and a trade happens whenever a new order crosses that gap.

title: Limit orders
text: A limit order tells the exchange to buy or sell only at a specified price or better. If the market never reaches that price, the order simply rests in the order book and may never fill. Traders use limit orders to control the price they pay, accepting the risk that the trade might not happen at all.

title: Market orders
text: A market order asks to trade immediately at the best available price. It almost always fills, but the final price is not guaranteed, especially when the order is large compared with the liquidity resting in the book. Large market orders can walk through several price levels and suffer meaningful slippage.

title: The bid-ask spread
text: The bid-ask spread is the difference between the highest price a buyer will pay and the lowest price a seller will accept. A narrow spread signals a liquid market with many participants competing. Wide spreads are a hidden cost of trading because a buyer who immediately sells loses the spread.

title: Market makers
text: Market makers continuously quote both a bid and an ask, earning the spread in exchange for providing liquidity. Their main risk is inventory: if prices move sharply while they hold a large position, the losses can exceed many days of spread income. Modern market making is almost entirely automated.

title: Liquidity
text: Liquidity describes how quickly an asset can be turned into cash without moving its price much. Cash itself is perfectly liquid, large company stocks are highly liquid, and real estate is relatively illiquid. During a crisis liquidity can vanish suddenly, which is why risk managers stress test for it.

title: ACH transfers
text: The Automated Clearing House network moves money between bank accounts in the United States in batches. Payroll deposits and utility bill payments typically travel over ACH. Transfers are cheap but not instant, and a payment can be returned days later if the account had insufficient funds.

title: Wire transfers
text: A wire transfer moves funds between banks individually rather than in batches, and it usually settles the same day. Wires cost more than ACH payments but are difficult to reverse once sent. That finality makes them useful for large purchases and also attractive to fraudsters running impersonation scams.

title: Card authorization and capture
text: When a card is swiped, the merchant first requests an authorization, which places a hold on the cardholder's available credit. Later the merchant captures the payment, often for a final amount that differs from the hold, such as a restaurant bill with a tip added. Separating authorization from capture lets merchants confirm funds before shipping goods.

title: Chargebacks
text: A chargeback happens when a cardholder disputes a transaction with their bank and the funds are pulled back from the merchant. Merchants can contest the dispute by submitting evidence such as delivery confirmations. A high chargeback rate can get a merchant dropped by its payment processor, so fraud prevention directly protects revenue.

title: Know your customer
text: Know your customer rules require financial companies to verify the identity of the people they serve. Typical checks include a government ID, a date of birth, and an address that can be matched against trusted records. Strong onboarding checks make it harder to open accounts with stolen or synthetic identities.

title: Anti-money laundering
text: Anti-money laundering programs watch for patterns that suggest criminal proceeds are being disguised as legitimate income. Classic red flags include many deposits just under a reporting threshold and money that moves rapidly through a chain of accounts. Suspicious activity must be reported to regulators rather than quietly ignored.

title: Fraud scoring
text: Fraud scoring assigns each transaction a risk score based on signals such as the amount, the device, the location, and how the purchase compares with the customer's normal behavior. Transactions above a threshold can be blocked or sent for manual review. The hard part is balancing missed fraud against the cost of declining honest customers.

title: Payment tokenization
text: Payment tokenization replaces a real card number with a substitute value that is useless if stolen. Only the token vault can map the token back to the original number. Mobile wallets use this technique, which is why a breach of a merchant database holding only tokens exposes far less sensitive data.

title: PCI DSS
text: The Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard is a set of rules for any company that stores, processes, or transmits card data. It covers network segmentation, encryption, access control, and regular security testing. Many startups reduce their compliance scope by letting a payment processor handle raw card numbers entirely.

title: Trade settlement
text: Settlement is the moment when securities and cash actually change hands after a trade. Stock trades in the United States now settle one business day after the trade date. A shorter settlement cycle reduces counterparty risk because less can go wrong between agreeing to a trade and completing it.

title: Clearing houses
text: A clearing house stands between the buyer and the seller of a trade and guarantees that both sides will be honored. It collects margin from members so that a single default does not cascade through the market. Netting is another benefit: offsetting trades cancel out, so far less cash needs to move.

title: Ledger reconciliation
text: Reconciliation compares an internal ledger with an external source of truth, such as a bank statement, and flags every difference. Mismatches can come from timing, fees nobody recorded, or outright bugs. Running reconciliation daily keeps small discrepancies from quietly growing into large unexplained losses.

title: Why floats are bad for money
text: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so adding ten cents and twenty cents can produce a value slightly different from thirty cents. Financial software therefore stores amounts as integer cents or uses a decimal type. A rounding error of a fraction of a cent becomes real money when repeated across millions of transactions.

title: Interest rate risk
text: Interest rate risk is the chance that changing rates will reduce the value of an investment. When rates rise, existing bonds that pay lower coupons become less attractive, so their prices fall. Banks face a version of this risk when they fund long-term loans with short-term deposits.

title: Bond duration
text: Duration measures how sensitive a bond's price is to a change in interest rates. A bond with a duration of seven years will lose roughly seven percent of its value if rates rise by one percentage point. Longer maturities and smaller coupons both increase duration.

title: The yield curve
text: The yield curve plots the interest rates on government bonds across different maturities. Normally longer bonds pay more because investors want compensation for tying up money. When short-term rates rise above long-term rates the curve is said to be inverted, a pattern that has often preceded recessions.

title: Inflation
text: Inflation is the gradual rise in the general price level, which means each unit of currency buys a little less over time. Moderate inflation is considered normal, but high inflation punishes savers and makes long-term planning difficult. Central banks usually respond to high inflation by raising interest rates.

title: Diversification
text: Diversification spreads money across many investments so that a single failure does not ruin the whole portfolio. It works because different assets rarely all fall at the same moment. Diversification reduces the risk specific to one company, but it cannot remove the risk that the entire market declines.

title: Index funds
text: An index fund tries to match the return of a market index rather than beat it. Because it simply holds what the index holds, its fees are usually much lower than those of actively managed funds. Over long periods low fees compound into a significant advantage for the investor.

title: Options contracts
text: An option gives its holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell an asset at a fixed strike price before an expiration date. A call option profits when the price rises and a put option profits when the price falls. The buyer pays a premium up front, which is the most they can lose.

title: Short selling
text: Short selling means borrowing shares, selling them, and hoping to buy them back later at a lower price. The potential loss is unlimited because there is no ceiling on how high a price can climb. Short sellers also pay a borrowing fee and can be forced to close positions during a short squeeze.

title: Stablecoins
text: A stablecoin is a digital token designed to hold a steady value, usually one dollar. Some are backed by cash and short-term government debt held in reserve, while others rely on algorithms or crypto collateral. Their stability is only as strong as the reserves and the redemption process behind them.

title: ACID database transactions
text: A database transaction groups several writes so that they either all succeed or all fail. The ACID properties are atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability. A money transfer is the classic example: debiting one account without crediting the other would be a serious bug, so both writes belong in the same transaction.

title: Event sourcing
text: Event sourcing stores every change to the system as an immutable event instead of overwriting the current state. The present state is rebuilt by replaying events in order. This gives a complete audit trail for free, which suits financial systems, at the cost of more complex queries and schema evolution.

title: Message queues
text: A message queue lets one service hand work to another without waiting for it to finish. If the consumer crashes, messages stay in the queue until it recovers. Most queues deliver at least once, so consumers must be written to handle duplicate messages safely, which brings us back to idempotency.

title: Rate limiting
text: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window. A common algorithm is the token bucket, where tokens refill at a steady rate and each request spends one. Limits protect an API from abuse and keep a single noisy client from degrading service for everyone else.

title: Caching
text: A cache keeps recently used data in fast storage so repeated reads avoid slow work. The difficult part is invalidation: deciding when a cached value is stale. Account balances are a risky thing to cache because showing an outdated number can lead customers to overdraw their accounts.

title: Database indexes
text: A database index is a separate data structure, often a B-tree, that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. Indexes make reads faster but slow down writes, since every insert must also update each index. Choosing indexes is a trade-off guided by the queries the application actually runs.

title: Latency and throughput
text: Latency is how long one request takes, while throughput is how many requests a system completes per second. Trading systems care intensely about tail latency, the slowest requests, because a delay of a few milliseconds can mean a worse price. Averages hide these outliers, so engineers track percentiles instead.

title: Two-factor authentication
text: Two-factor authentication requires a second proof of identity beyond a password, such as a code from an authenticator app. Even if a password leaks, an attacker still needs the second factor. Banks increasingly prefer app-based codes or hardware keys over text messages, which can be intercepted through SIM swapping.

title: Password hashing
text: Passwords should never be stored in plain text. Instead a system stores a slow, salted hash produced by an algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2. The salt prevents attackers from using precomputed tables, and the deliberate slowness makes guessing billions of passwords expensive.

title: JSON Web Tokens
text: A JSON Web Token is a signed bundle of claims that a server can verify without a database lookup. That makes it convenient for stateless APIs, but it also means a token cannot easily be revoked before it expires. Short expiration times combined with refresh tokens are a common compromise.

title: Encryption at rest
text: Encryption at rest protects stored data, such as database files and backups, so that a stolen disk reveals nothing useful. The encryption keys must live somewhere separate, usually a key management service. Encryption in transit is a different concern that covers data moving across the network.

title: Credit scores
text: A credit score summarizes how reliably a person has repaid debt in the past. Payment history and the share of available credit currently in use carry the most weight. Lenders use the score to decide whether to approve a loan and what interest rate to charge.
